html:
The Warring States period was the last part of the Zhou era in China, from about 475 BCE until the state of Qin united the country in 221 BCE. The Zhou king still reigned but had no power. Seven large states fought for mastery: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei.

War changed in scale. Iron tools made farming richer and states bigger. Rulers raised huge armies of conscript foot soldiers armed with crossbows, built long border walls, the forerunners of the Great Wall, and replaced old nobles with paid officials. Smaller states vanished, such as Yue, broken by Chu.

It was also China's great age of thought, the "Hundred Schools":

  • Mencius carried on the teaching of Confucius.
  • The Tao Te Ching, credited to Laozi, took shape.
  • Mozi preached universal love and against offensive war.
  • Legalists such as Shang Yang and Han Fei taught rule by strict law, rewards and punishments.
  • The Art of War, credited to Sun Tzu, set down military strategy.

Qin took up Legalist reforms from the 350s BCE and grew into the strongest state. Between 230 and 221 BCE its king conquered the other six (Qin unifies China) and took the title First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
